clips.asr_text: Today's topic is The Open Window.
Frampton is visiting a family in the country when he meets Vera, a young girl with a story to tell. As the visit continues, listen for how her story shapes what Framton thinks and how he responds.
Listen for what Vera says about the open window.
Vera says her aunt still waits for her husband and brothers to return. What will Framton think when he hears the aunt speak about them?
Vera told Frampton that her aunt was waiting for her husband and brothers to return. What does Frampton see when he turns toward the lawn?
Give way.
to break or collapse under pressure.
At a moment's notice.
With almost no warning or preparation.
Keep someone company.
To spend time with someone so they are not alone.
Frampton sat on the edge of his chair, turning his letter of introduction between his fingers. His doctor had recommended peace and country air, but visiting strangers was hardly peaceful.
My aunt will be down soon.
said Vera, her fifteen-year-old niece.
Do you know much about her?
Almost nothing.
he admitted. Vera glanced towards the French window, which stood wide open to the lawn.
Her great tragedy happened three years ago today.
Frampton stopped turning the letter.

Her husband and her two young brothers went out shooting through that window. Their little brown spaniel went with them. They tried to cross the bog, but the ground gave way beneath them. They all disappeared. Their bodies were never found.
How terrible!
Frampton murmured.
My aunt still thinks they'll come back. She keeps the window open until dark, waiting for them.
Vera's voice grew quieter.
She looked out across the empty lawn.
Sometimes on evenings like this, I almost expect to see them.
Before Frampton could reply, her aunt hurried into the room.
I hope Vera has kept you company. You don't mind the open window. My husband and brothers will be back soon. They've been shooting. Their boots will be covered in mud, of course.

Crampton felt a chill, so she really was waiting. He began describing his illness, trying to keep his eyes away from the window. His hostess listened with only half her attention. Again and again she looked past him towards the lawn. Then her face brightened.
Here they are at last!
Vera stared outside, her eyes wide with horror. Framton turned.
Three figures were crossing the lawn in the fading light, carrying guns. A white coat hung over one man's arm, a brown spaniel followed close behind. Across the quiet garden came a young voice.

Frampton could scarcely breathe. The dead were coming towards the house. He grabbed his hat and stick and rushed out. Within seconds, he was running down the drive. The men stepped through the window, muddy and hungry.
Who was that?
asked the husband.
A most peculiar visitor.
His wife said.
He talked about his nerves, then suddenly ran away.
It was the spaniel.
Vera said calmly.
He told me he was terrified of dogs. In India, a pack chased him into an empty grave. He spent the whole night there with them snarling above him.
Inventing convincing stories at a moment's notice was Vera's forte.
